issues.legal_issue: The identity of the person who constructed a shade over leased ground must be determined before deciding whether the eviction dispute is governed by the rent statute and can be resolved on that basis.
material_facts: The tenants occupied shop premises consisting of ground beneath a tin shade, but there was no finding whether the landlords or the tenants had constructed the shade.

The trial court treated the premises as a building under the rent statute, while the appellate court treated them as outside the statute and ordered eviction without deciding who had constructed the shade.
If the tenants had constructed the shade, the lease would be of open ground rather than of a building.
issues.conclusion: The question of who constructed the shade must be determined first, with the eviction issue considered thereafter. The lower courts’ decisions were set aside and the matter remanded for that determination and a fresh decision on the appeal.
issues.legal_principle: Under Section 3(i) of the U.P. Urban Buildings (Regulation of Letting, Rent and Eviction) Act, 1972, whether the premises are a building affects the forum and governing procedure. If the tenants constructed the shade, the lease would be of open land, which is not a building within that provision. The identity of the builder therefore must be resolved before deciding the eviction dispute; the Court did not decide whether the shade itself was a building.

predicates.eviction_appeal: The proceeding is an appeal concerning an eviction dispute.
predicates.leased_ground_has_shade: The leased premises include ground beneath a shade or similar structure.
predicates.shade_builder_not_found: The lower court has not found whether the landlord or tenant constructed the shade.
predicates.builder_identity_must_be_determined_befo: The identity of the person who constructed the shade must be determined before the eviction dispute is decided.

issues.definition: When an eviction appeal concerns leased ground beneath a shade and the lower court has not found who built it, the builder’s identity must be determined before the eviction dispute is decided.

issues.legal_issue: A decision concerning a lease of open land on which the tenant was permitted to construct a removable shed does not determine the status of premises let with a shade whose builder is unknown.
material_facts: The earlier decision concerned open land let to a tenant who was permitted to construct a tin shed and could remove its materials on leaving.
In this case, the leased ground had a tin shade over it, and there was no finding whether the landlord or tenant had constructed that shade.
issues.conclusion: The earlier decision does not apply to these facts.
issues.legal_principle: The Court distinguished Narayan Chand Dass v. Panna Lal and Anr.: that case concerned a lease of open land and a shed constructed by the tenant with removable materials, whereas the present case concerned ground let with a shade whose builder had not been identified. The question whether the shade constituted a building under Section 3(i) of the U.P. Urban Buildings (Regulation of Letting, Rent and Eviction) Act, 1972, remained undecided.

predicates.cited_decision_tenant_built_removable_sh: In the earlier decision, the tenant was permitted to build a shed and could remove its materials on leaving.
predicates.present_lease_included_shade_of_unknown_: The present lease concerned ground beneath a shade whose builder had not been identified.
predicates.cited_decision_does_not_apply: The earlier decision does not govern the dispute.

issues.definition: An earlier decision about open land with a tenant-built removable shed does not apply where the lease included ground beneath a shade of unknown origin and the statute’s application is disputed.
